Automating existing gates typically takes one to two days. Underground motors and new gate installations take longer because of the groundworks.
Looking after electric swing gates

Have the gates serviced once a year. A service covers checking the motors and safety devices, testing the closing force, adjusting the travel limits, greasing the hinges and testing the battery backup. Between services, keep the photocell lenses clean and the area behind the gates clear. See gate repair and servicing if anything starts behaving oddly.

faqs.question: Should swing gates open inward?
faqs.answer: Almost always, if the gate is on the boundary with a public pavement or road. Outward opening is only possible over private land, and the arc still needs to be kept clear of anywhere people walk.

faqs.question: What width should I choose?
faqs.answer: At least 3 metres for a car, and 3.5 to 4 metres if you’re turning in from a narrow street. Make sure there’s space behind the gates for the leaves to open with your car parked beyond them.

faqs.question: Are swing gates cheaper than sliding gates?
faqs.answer: Usually, because they need less groundwork. But a swing gate on a slope or tight drive can need costly workarounds, and then a sliding gate can cost about the same.

faqs.question: Can you automate my existing gates?
faqs.answer: Often, yes, if the gates are rigid, the hinges are sound and the piers are strong enough. See gate automation retrofits.

faqs.question: What happens in a power cut?
faqs.answer: 24V systems can run on battery backup for a number of cycles. Otherwise, each leaf can be released with a key and opened by hand.

faqs.question: How long do the gates take to open?
faqs.answer: Typically 15 to 25 seconds, depending on leaf length and motor type.

wooden-driveway-gates.title: Wooden Driveway Gates
wooden-driveway-gates.description: Timber driveway gates for London homes, with the species, construction, finish and upkeep agreed before ordering.
sections: Which timber?

Treated softwood (usually redwood or pine) is the budget option. It’s pressure-treated against rot, takes paint well and keeps costs down. It’s also less stable than hardwood, so it’s more likely to twist or shrink, and it needs regular repainting to last. With good care, expect something like 10 to 15 years.

European oak is the traditional choice for period and country-style gates. It’s very strong, heavy and naturally durable, and left unfinished it weathers to a soft silver-grey. Oak contains tannins that react with ordinary steel, causing black staining around fixings and on pale paving in the first year or two. Proper oak gates use stainless steel or galvanised fittings for that reason. Oak also moves and develops small surface cracks (known as checks) as it dries, which is normal.

Iroko and other tropical hardwoods such as sapele give a rich golden-brown colour, high natural durability and better stability than oak, often at a lower price. Ask for FSC or PEFC certification, which shows the timber comes from responsibly managed forests.

Western red cedar is light, stable and naturally rot-resistant, with a warm reddish tone. Its lightness makes it easy to automate, but it’s soft and dents more easily than hardwood.

Accoya is sustainably grown pine that’s been chemically modified so it barely absorbs water. It’s one of the most stable and durable timbers available. It holds paint for much longer than ordinary wood, and the manufacturer offers a long warranty on the timber itself. It costs more than most hardwoods, but suits painted gates that you want to stay straight and crisp for decades. Our Accoya guide explains how the timber warranty differs from a warranty on the finished gate.
How a good wooden gate is built

Most cheap wooden gates fail at the joints, or through sagging. A well-made gate has a frame joined with mortise and tenon joints, glued and pegged, not screwed or nailed. Diagonal braces run upwards from the bottom hinge to the top of the latch side, so they carry the weight back to the hinges. Fitted the wrong way round, they do nothing. The boarding is tongue-and-groove or properly spaced, so the timber can swell and shrink with the seasons without splitting or bowing.

Large gates, and any gate that’s going to be automated, benefit from laminated stiles (the vertical frame members), which are made from several bonded layers and resist twisting. Very large or heavy gates can be built around a hidden galvanised steel frame clad in timber, so the leaves never sag however wide they are.
Design options

Solid boarded gates with a flat, arched or swan-neck top are the classic choice for period homes and give full privacy. Gates with an open top section of spindles or a fretwork panel let you see the road as you leave and look less imposing from the street. Horizontal slatted designs, often in iroko, cedar or Accoya, suit contemporary houses. Hardware matters too. Black forged hinges and ring handles look right on a traditional gate, while concealed hinges and slim stainless fittings suit a modern one.
Finish and upkeep

You have three realistic choices. Paint (a microporous system that lets the timber breathe) gives a crisp colour and good protection, and needs recoating every few years depending on timber and exposure. Accoya extends that interval considerably. A translucent oil or stain shows the grain and is easy to refresh, but needs reapplying more often, typically every year or two on south-facing gates. Leaving hardwood unfinished to silver naturally is the lowest-maintenance option, as long as you’re happy with the grey colour and some surface checking.

Whatever finish you choose, it should be applied in the workshop to every face of the gate, including the end grain and the edges that won’t be visible once the gate is hung. The end grain soaks up water like a straw if it’s left bare, and that’s where rot starts. A quick wash down each spring and a check of the finish on the bottom rail, which takes the worst of the rain splash, will add years to any wooden gate.
Automating a wooden gate

Timber gates automate well, with a few conditions. Solid hardwood is heavy, and a solid oak leaf can easily weigh more than 100 kg. A solid boarded gate also catches the wind, so the motor has to be sized for both the weight and the wind load, not the weight alone. The gate needs a rigid frame that won’t sag or twist. Otherwise it will drift out of alignment with the motor and the closing stop.

For period homes, underground motors are popular because they’re hidden in the ground beneath the hinge and leave the gate looking traditional. Ram motors mounted on the inside face are the most common and economical choice. Articulated arm motors suit deep brick piers where a ram won’t fit. See electric swing gates for how these compare. If you already have a wooden gate you’d like to motorise, see gate automation retrofits. We’ll check the gate is sound enough first.
Posts and piers

Hanging a heavy wooden gate on undersized posts or crumbling brick is the quickest way to make it sag. Timber posts should be substantial hardwood, typically 200 mm square or more for driveway gates, set deep in concrete. On brick piers, hinges are fixed with resin anchors into sound brickwork. Some old piers need rebuilding or reinforcing before they can carry a new gate, and we check that at survey rather than discovering it on installation day.
Planning permission

Under permitted development rules, gates next to a road or footpath can usually be up to 1 metre high without planning permission. Anything taller needs consent. Conservation areas, listed buildings and properties with Article 4 directions (which remove some permitted development rights) have stricter rules. Our borough planning guides cover the local position. In many conservation areas, a well-designed timber gate gets a smoother reception than metal.
Cost of wooden driveway gates in London

As a rough guide, a pair of treated softwood driveway gates typically costs £1,200 to £2,500 supplied and fitted. Hardwood such as iroko or oak usually runs from £3,000 to £7,000 for a pair, depending on size and design, and Accoya sits at or slightly above that. Automation typically adds £2,500 to £6,000, depending on motor type, with underground motors at the top of that range. New posts, rebuilt piers and groundworks are quoted separately. Our gate cost guide has more detail.

faqs.question: How long do wooden gates last?
faqs.answer: It depends mostly on the timber and how well it’s looked after. Treated softwood typically lasts 10 to 15 years with regular painting. Good hardwood and Accoya gates commonly last 25 years or more. Joinery quality and how well the end grain is sealed matter as much as the species.

faqs.question: Can wooden gates be automated?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the gate is rigid and the motor is sized for its weight and wind load. Heavy solid gates and wide leaves need more powerful motors, and gates with a weak frame should be rebuilt before they’re automated.

faqs.question: Which timber should I choose?
faqs.answer: For a painted gate you want to stay straight with minimal fuss, choose Accoya. For a traditional natural look on a period property, oak or iroko. For a lighter contemporary slatted gate, cedar or iroko. On a tight budget, treated softwood is the sensible choice. We bring samples to the survey so you can see each one against your house.

faqs.question: Will my wooden gate warp?
faqs.answer: All timber moves a little with the seasons, so boards may show small gaps in summer and tighten in winter. Proper joinery, stable timbers and laminated stiles keep that movement from becoming warping or sagging.

faqs.question: Wood or aluminium?
faqs.answer: Aluminium is lighter, needs almost no maintenance and is available in convincing wood-effect finishes. Real timber looks and feels better on many period homes. Our wooden and aluminium comparison covers the trade-offs, and our hardwood gates page goes deeper on oak and iroko.

metal-driveway-gates.title: Metal Driveway Gates
metal-driveway-gates.description: Compare metal driveway gate designs, fabrication and finish options for your London entrance.
sections: What metal gates are actually made of

Almost every “wrought iron” gate sold today is made from mild steel. True wrought iron hasn’t been produced commercially for decades and only survives in reclaimed and antique work. Mild steel is strong, easy to shape into scrolls and bars, and can be welded and repaired. Its weakness is rust, so the finish matters more than anything else.

Aluminium is far lighter than steel and doesn’t rust, which makes it a natural fit for wide gates, sliding gates and automation. It’s usually powder-coated and suits contemporary slatted and panel designs particularly well. Decorative aluminium castings let it imitate traditional styles too. See aluminium driveway gates for more.

Some modern gates also use stainless steel for a bright architectural look, or weathering steel (often sold as Corten), which develops a stable rust-coloured surface by design.
How the finish protects the gate

This is where cheap metal gates and good ones differ most. The gold standard for steel is hot-dip galvanising followed by powder coating, often called a duplex finish. The finished gate is dipped in molten zinc, which coats it inside and out, including the welds and the insides of hollow bars where rust usually starts. A powder coat is then baked on top for colour. A duplex-finished gate commonly lasts 25 years or more before it needs any serious attention.

Powder coat applied straight onto bare steel looks identical on the day of installation. Once it chips, though, water gets underneath and rust creeps along the steel under the coating, typically showing first at welds and the bottom rail within a few years. Wet-painted steel is cheaper still and needs repainting regularly. When comparing quotes, ask exactly which of these you’re getting, and whether galvanising is done after all the welding.

Colour is personal, but black remains the classic for traditional gates and anthracite grey (RAL 7016) has become the default for contemporary ones. Satin and textured finishes hide fingerprints and marks better than gloss. Our colour trends article has examples.
Choosing a design

Traditional designs include straight-top, arched and swan-neck (concave) gates, with vertical bars finished in spear, ball or fleur-de-lis tops and details such as collars and scrolls. These suit period houses and are often what conservation areas expect. Bow-top gates give a softer, rounded look.

Contemporary designs lean on horizontal slats or flat bars, solid or perforated sheet panels, and laser-cut patterns. The gap between slats decides how much privacy you get and how much of the road you can see as you pull out. Our slat gate guide goes into spacing and sightlines. For full privacy with a softer look, a steel frame with timber or composite infill combines the strength of metal with the warmth of wood.

If you have children or a dog, keep gaps between bars and under the gate below 100 mm so they can’t squeeze through or get stuck. Horizontal rails on the outside face make a gate easy to climb, so on security-conscious frontages they’re best kept on the inside.
Posts, hinges and weight

A pair of steel driveway gates can weigh several hundred kilograms, so they need solid supports. Steel box-section posts concreted into the ground are the most reliable option. Existing brick piers can be used if they’re sound, with hinges fixed into the brickwork with resin anchors. Adjustable hinges (or ball-bearing hinges on heavier gates) let the leaves be realigned if anything settles over time. Aluminium gates put much less load on posts and piers, which can make them a better choice where the existing brickwork is weak.
Automation

Metal gates automate very well. The best results come when automation is planned before fabrication: motor brackets and fixing points are welded on before the gate is galvanised, so nothing needs drilling or welding afterwards that breaks the protective coating. Steel swing gates suit ram, articulated arm or underground motors. Where space is tight, a metal gate can be built as a sliding gate instead. See electric swing gates, electric sliding gates and our swing vs sliding guide.
Restoring old metal gates

Original Victorian and Edwardian gates are often worth saving, especially on listed buildings and in conservation areas, where the planners may expect them to stay. Restoration usually means removing the gates, blast-cleaning back to bare metal, repairing or recasting damaged sections, then refinishing. Steel can be galvanised. Cast iron is usually primed with a zinc-rich primer instead, because the heat of galvanising can crack it. Our restoration article and wrought iron gates page cover this in more detail.
Planning permission

Under permitted development, gates next to a road or footpath can usually be up to 1 metre high without planning permission. Taller gates need consent, and conservation areas, listed buildings and Article 4 directions (which remove some permitted development rights) add further restrictions. See our borough planning guides.
Looking after a metal gate

A galvanised and powder-coated gate needs very little care. Wash it down with water and mild detergent once or twice a year, particularly near main roads where traffic grime builds up. Touch up any chips with a zinc-rich primer and matching topcoat before rust can start. Grease the hinges and check the fixings annually. If it’s automated, have the motors and safety devices serviced too.
Cost of metal driveway gates in London

As a rough guide, a pair of made-to-measure galvanised and powder-coated steel driveway gates typically costs £2,500 to £6,000 supplied and fitted, depending on width and design. Highly ornate or fully bespoke work can be £6,000 to £12,000 or more. Aluminium gates are generally similar to slightly higher for the same design. Automation usually adds £2,500 to £6,000. New posts, pier repairs and groundworks are quoted separately. Our gate cost guide has more detail.

faqs.question: Are all metal gates galvanised?
faqs.answer: No, and many cheaper gates aren’t. Ask whether the gate is hot-dip galvanised after fabrication, then powder-coated. That combination is what keeps rust away for decades.

faqs.question: Is a “wrought iron” gate really wrought iron?
faqs.answer: Almost certainly not, unless it’s antique. Modern iron-style gates are mild steel, which is just as good-looking and easier to repair.

faqs.question: Steel or aluminium?
faqs.answer: Steel is stronger, heavier and better for intricate traditional ironwork. Aluminium is lighter, can’t rust, and is better for wide gates, weak piers and sliding gates. Both can be made in traditional or modern styles.

faqs.question: Can you restore an existing iron gate?
faqs.answer: Usually, yes. We check whether it’s steel, wrought iron or cast iron and how much corrosion there is, then advise whether restoration or replacement makes more sense.

faqs.question: Are metal gates maintenance-free?
faqs.answer: Not quite, but close if they’re galvanised and powder-coated. An occasional wash, touching up chips and greasing the hinges once a year is usually all they need.

anpr-systems.title: ANPR Gate Entry Systems
anpr-systems.description: Number-plate entry planned around camera position, authorised vehicles, safe waiting and access-data management.
sections: How ANPR works

A dedicated ANPR camera watches the approach to the gate. It uses infrared light to read the reflective number plate clearly, day or night. Software reads the registration and checks it against a list of authorised vehicles. If it matches, the system sends an open signal to the gate’s control panel, exactly like pressing a remote. Unknown plates are ignored, logged, or passed to an intercom so the driver can call the house or reception.

This isn’t ordinary CCTV with software added. ANPR cameras use fast shutters and infrared lighting tuned to reading plates. A general security camera pointed at the drive will struggle, especially at night and with moving cars.
Camera position makes or breaks it

Most of an ANPR system’s reliability comes down to where the camera goes. It needs a clear view of the front plate as the car approaches, from a fairly shallow angle. It’s typically mounted on a post or wall at around bumper-to-roof height, 3 to 10 metres from where the car will be when the plate is read. Too steep an angle, a camera looking into low sun or headlights, or a bend in the approach all reduce read rates. We survey the approach, test the position and set up the camera on site with real vehicles before handover.
How reliable is it?

A well-installed system reads clean, standard UK plates very reliably. Reads fail on dirty or damaged plates, plates partly hidden by a towbar or bike rack, and illegal “show plates” with altered fonts or spacing. Foreign plates may also be missed. Motorbikes have no front plate, so they need another way in, or a camera placed to read the rear. That’s why every ANPR installation should keep a backup: a remote, keypad, GSM phone entry or intercom, so a missed read is a minor inconvenience, not a locked-out driver.
What it’s like to drive in

With a barrier, ANPR feels almost seamless. The barrier opens in a few seconds and most cars barely stop. With a swing or sliding gate, the gate still takes 15 to 25 seconds to open, so you’ll usually wait a short time unless the camera reads your plate well before you reach the gate. Placing the camera further down the approach helps where there’s room. Either way, the gate is designed to open fully before you drive through, and the car should never be waiting on the pavement or road. Exit is usually automatic, triggered by a sensor loop in the drive or an exit button, so you don’t need a second camera unless you want exit logs.
Managing vehicles

You manage the list of authorised plates through an app or web portal. Good systems make the everyday changes simple. You can add a new car, remove a sold one, or give a builder’s van access for the next three weeks only. Visitors expected on a particular day can be added with an expiry time, so their access stops automatically. Unknown vehicles can trigger the intercom or send a notification to your phone with a photo, so you can let them in with a tap. Many systems also tell you when a family member’s car has arrived home.

For residential developments and commercial sites, sort out early who has permission to add and remove plates, how residents or staff register a new car, and how quickly leavers are removed. A list that’s never reviewed gradually lets in people who should no longer have access.
Visitors and deliveries

ANPR handles vehicles you know about. For everyone else, pair it with an intercom placed where a visiting driver can reach it from the car window. Couriers and delivery drivers usually come in unknown vans, so a video intercom or GSM intercom that rings your phone is the practical answer. Our parcel delivery access guide covers this in more detail.
Local or cloud-based

Some ANPR systems do everything on the camera or a small unit on site, so they keep working if your internet goes down. Others use a cloud service for the plate list, the app and the logs, which makes remote management easy but adds a monthly subscription and depends on your connection. Many systems combine the two: plates are checked locally and synced from the cloud. We’ll explain which parts of the system you’re paying for monthly, and what still works if the subscription ends or the broadband fails.
Data protection

Number plates are personal data. On commercial sites and residential developments, the site operator is responsible for using ANPR lawfully under UK GDPR. That means signs telling drivers ANPR is in use, a clear reason for collecting the data, a set retention period for plate images and logs, and control over who can see them. For a private home, the ICO’s guidance is that data protection law applies if the camera captures images beyond your own property boundary, such as the public road. We aim cameras to cover your approach and as little of the street as possible, and set sensible retention periods by default. The ICO’s guidance on video surveillance sets out the full requirements.
Safety

ANPR decides whether a car is allowed to enter. It doesn’t decide whether the gate is safe to move. That’s still the job of the gate’s photocells, safety edges and force limits, tested to BS EN 12453. ANPR also doesn’t stop a second car following the first through an open gate, so on sites where tailgating matters, the gate or barrier should close promptly behind each vehicle.
Cost of ANPR gate entry in London

As a rough guide, adding ANPR to an existing electric gate at a home typically costs £1,500 to £3,500 installed, including the camera, set-up and integration. Commercial and multi-lane installations are usually £2,500 to £6,000 per lane. Cloud-managed systems usually carry an ongoing subscription, often somewhere between £10 and £50 a month depending on features and the number of vehicles. Every quote sets out the equipment, installation and ongoing costs separately.

faqs.question: Will ANPR read every plate?
faqs.answer: It will read the vast majority of clean, standard UK plates when the camera is well positioned. Dirty, damaged, non-standard and foreign plates can fail, which is why a backup entry method is always included.

faqs.question: Can cars drive straight in without stopping?
faqs.answer: With a fast barrier, nearly. With a swing or sliding gate, expect a short wait while the gate opens, unless the camera can read the plate well before you reach it.

faqs.question: Does it work at night?
faqs.answer: Yes. ANPR cameras use infrared lighting and read plates in complete darkness.

faqs.question: What about motorbikes?
faqs.answer: Motorbikes only have a rear plate, so a front-facing camera won’t read them. Use a remote or keypad, or a camera positioned to read the rear plate.

faqs.question: What happens when I change my car?
faqs.answer: Remove the old registration and add the new one in the app. It takes seconds.

faqs.question: Does ANPR replace the gate’s safety devices?
faqs.answer: No. It only sends the open command. Photocells, safety edges and force testing are still required.

video-intercoms.title: Video Intercom Systems
video-intercoms.description: See and speak to visitors through a video-entry system specified for your gate, network and household.
sections: How it works

A visitor presses the call button on a panel at the gate. The panel has a camera, microphone and speaker. The call rings on one or more screens inside the house and, on most modern systems, on your phone through an app. You see and speak to the visitor, then press a button to open the driveway gate, the pedestrian gate or both. The intercom simply tells the gate’s control panel to open, just like a remote. The gate’s own safety devices still control how it moves.
Types of system

Two-wire systems send video, audio and power along a single pair of cables. They’re robust and reliable over long distances, often more than 100 metres, which suits long drives. They’re also ideal where an old intercom cable already runs from the gate to the house and can be reused. Comelit, Videx and Fermax all make well-regarded two-wire ranges. Many now add app calling through a gateway unit.

IP systems run over network cable, usually a single external-grade Cat6 cable carrying data and power (Power over Ethernet) up to about 100 metres. They give the sharpest video, app calling, multiple monitors, recording and easy integration with CCTV, and are increasingly the default for new installations. Hikvision, Akuvox, 2N and DoorBird are common choices.

Wireless and Wi-Fi systems avoid digging a cable trench, but a gate is often 20 to 50 metres from the house, sometimes behind brick walls and metal gates. Home Wi-Fi rarely reaches reliably. Where trenching isn’t practical, a point-to-point wireless link (a pair of small dishes) is far more dependable than Wi-Fi. For gates with no cable route at all, a 4G video intercom works over the mobile network instead. See GSM phone entry.
Getting the signal to the house

Most of the work in a video intercom installation is the cable route. The cable runs in a duct, usually under the drive or along a boundary, from the gate to the point where it enters the house. If you’re having the drive relaid or new gates installed, put the duct in then. It costs far less than lifting paving later. We survey the route, check any existing cables and agree where the indoor monitor and network connection will go before quoting.
The gate panel

Choose an external panel built for life outdoors on a street. It should be weatherproof (IP65 or better) and vandal-resistant, with a wide-angle camera, infrared night vision so you can see faces after dark, and wide dynamic range so a visitor isn’t just a silhouette against bright sky or headlights. Panels can include a keypad or fob reader, so the same unit handles visitors and residents.

Mount the panel at around 1.4 to 1.5 metres for people on foot. For drivers, fit a second panel on a gooseneck post at car-window height, or mount it where the driver can reach it without leaving the car or stopping across the pavement. On commercial sites, a third panel at lorry-cab height is common. See car park barriers.
Inside the house

Indoor monitors range from simple 4 or 7-inch screens to 10-inch touchscreens that can also show CCTV cameras. You can have several, such as one in the kitchen, one upstairs and one in a home office, and they can all ring together or in sequence. Monitors can also act as an internal intercom between rooms.
Answering on your phone

App calling forwards the call to your phone, so you can let in a delivery driver or cleaner while you’re out. It relies on the gate panel having a network connection and your phone getting the notification. Expect a few seconds’ delay compared with an indoor monitor, and make sure the system will still ring the indoor monitor if your broadband goes down. Some apps need a subscription for remote access or cloud recordings. We’ll tell you exactly what’s included before you buy.
Linking to the gate

The intercom connects to the gate’s control panel to open the gate. It can also connect to a second relay for an electric lock on a pedestrian gate. Most modern gate control panels from the main manufacturers accept an intercom without difficulty. Older or unusual ones sometimes need an interface or an upgrade, which we check at survey. If you want the intercom to show whether the gate is actually open or closed, that needs a gate position sensor wired back to the intercom, and not every system supports it.
Recording and privacy

Many systems save a snapshot or short video clip each time someone calls, either on a memory card in the monitor, on a recorder or in the cloud. That’s useful for checking deliveries and visitors you missed. If the camera captures images beyond your property, such as the street or a neighbour’s house, data protection law applies even at home. The ICO’s guidance on domestic CCTV explains your responsibilities. We angle cameras to cover the visitor, not the pavement opposite, and many panels let you mask out areas you don’t want recorded.
Rough costs of video intercom systems in London

As a rough guide, a two-wire video intercom with one indoor monitor, connected to an existing gate, typically costs £900 to £2,000 installed. IP systems with app calling and multiple monitors usually cost £1,500 to £3,500. Premium panels with integrated keypads, fob readers and high-end cameras run £2,500 to £5,000. Trenching, ducting and reinstating the drive are itemised separately, and any app or cloud subscriptions are shown in the quote. Our intercom buying guide and Comelit vs Hikvision comparison go into the brands in more detail.

faqs.question: Can a video intercom work with my existing gate?
faqs.answer: Almost always, with modern gate control panels. Older or unusual control panels sometimes need an interface. We check the make and model at survey.

faqs.question: Can I answer the gate from my phone?
faqs.answer: Yes, with an IP system or a two-wire system with an app gateway. You’ll need broadband at the house (or a 4G intercom), and some apps charge a subscription.

faqs.question: Do I need a cable from the gate to the house?
faqs.answer: For the most reliable system, yes, run in a duct. Where that’s not possible, a point-to-point wireless link or a 4G intercom are good alternatives. Home Wi-Fi usually isn’t reliable enough.

faqs.question: Can I reuse my old intercom cable?
faqs.answer: Often, with a two-wire system designed for exactly that. We test the existing cable first.

faqs.question: Does it record visitors?
faqs.answer: Many systems save a snapshot or clip for every call. Continuous recording usually needs a CCTV recorder. Check which you’re getting before you buy.

faqs.question: Can it open a pedestrian gate too?
faqs.answer: Yes. Most intercoms have two outputs, one for the driveway gate and one for a pedestrian gate lock.

gsm-phone-entry.title: GSM Phone Entry Systems
gsm-phone-entry.description: Phone-based gate entry with the device, signal, SIM plan and user permissions checked for your entrance.
sections: Two kinds of GSM system

A GSM gate opener is a small unit wired into the gate’s control panel. You store a list of authorised phone numbers in it. When one of those numbers calls the unit, it recognises the caller ID, rejects the call and opens the gate. The call is never answered, so it normally costs the caller nothing. Calls from unknown numbers are ignored. It’s the simplest and cheapest way to give lots of people keyless access.

A GSM intercom adds a call panel at the gate for visitors. When someone presses the button, the unit rings your mobile (and then other numbers in turn if you don’t answer). You talk to the visitor and press a key on your phone to open the gate. Most GSM intercoms also work as an opener for authorised numbers. Video versions send a live picture to an app on your phone; see video intercoms.
Managing who can get in

Depending on the model, a GSM unit holds anywhere from a few hundred to several thousand phone numbers. Better units let you restrict numbers to set days and times (a cleaner on Tuesday mornings only), set numbers to expire on a date, and keep a log of who opened the gate and when. Most are managed by text message, a phone app or a web portal, so you can add or remove someone in seconds from wherever you are. When a carer or tenant leaves, you delete their number and their access stops immediately.

Some units can also tell you whether the gate actually opened. They do this by connecting to the gate’s position sensor and texting you a confirmation. That’s worth having if you open the gate remotely for deliveries and can’t see it.
The network switch-off

“GSM” originally meant the 2G mobile network, and many gate units still run on it. UK networks have now switched off 3G, and 2G will follow. The government’s agreement with the operators keeps 2G running until 2033 at the latest, but some services may wind down sooner. A unit bought today should be a 4G model, ideally one that supports voice calls over 4G (VoLTE), so it isn’t left stranded when older networks close. If you have an older 3G unit, it has almost certainly already stopped working. Ofcom’s switch-off guidance has the background.
SIM cards and running costs

The unit needs a SIM card that supports the services it uses: voice calls for opening and intercom calls, and texts for programming and alerts. Data is also needed for app-based models. A cheap SIM-only contract of a few pounds a month is the most reliable choice. Pay-as-you-go SIMs work, but many networks deactivate them if they’re not topped up or used for several months. A pay-as-you-go SIM in a gate that’s only opened by free rejected calls can quietly expire. Auto top-up avoids that. Intercom calls to your mobile come out of the gate SIM’s allowance, so busy entrances need a plan with enough minutes.

We record who owns the SIM and the admin account at handover. That way, if you move house or change installers, control of the system goes with the property and not with whoever set it up.
Signal, power and reliability

The unit only works as well as the mobile signal where it’s installed. Before installation, we test signal strength on the network you’ll use, in the exact position of the unit. A good signal on your own phone in the house is not the same test. Gate posts, metal enclosures and basement car parks can block reception. Where signal is weak, an external antenna on a short cable to a better spot usually solves it, or a different network can be used.

GSM entry doesn’t depend on home Wi-Fi or broadband, which is its big advantage over Wi-Fi gate systems. It does still need power. If the gate has battery backup, the GSM unit can usually run from it during a power cut. For the rare network outage, keep a remote or keypad as a backup way in. See keypad entry.
Security

GSM entry is as secure as the phones on its list. Keep the list up to date and remove numbers as soon as someone no longer needs access. Caller ID can in principle be faked, so for higher-security properties choose a unit that can require a PIN code during the call, or app control with proper log-in. Pairing GSM with a video intercom means you can see who you’re letting in rather than relying on a voice.
Where GSM works well

GSM entry suits homes with lots of regular visitors, holiday lets and Airbnb properties, where guest numbers can be added for the length of a stay. It’s also popular for elderly relatives with carers visiting at different times, shared driveways and small blocks of flats, and rural or outbuilding gates where broadband doesn’t reach. It works with any modern electric gate or barrier, including swing gates, sliding gates and car park barriers.
Cost of GSM phone entry in London

As a rough guide, a 4G GSM gate opener added to an existing electric gate typically costs £400 to £900 installed. An audio GSM intercom with a call panel is usually £900 to £1,800, and a 4G video intercom with app control £1,500 to £3,000. Add the SIM plan, usually a few pounds a month. Extra cabling, antennas and battery backup are itemised in the quote. Established makers such as AES, Videx and 2N all offer UK-supported 4G units.

faqs.question: Will any SIM card work?
faqs.answer: Most standard SIMs from the main networks work, as long as the plan covers voice and text and suits the unit. Avoid data-only SIMs, and be careful with pay-as-you-go SIMs that expire if they’re not used.

faqs.question: Does it cost anything to open the gate?
faqs.answer: With a standard GSM opener, no. The unit rejects your call, so it isn’t answered or charged. Intercom calls from the gate to your mobile use the gate SIM’s minutes.

faqs.question: Do I need broadband or Wi-Fi?
faqs.answer: No. The unit uses the mobile network. It does need power, and a mobile signal at the gate.

faqs.question: Will the network switch-off affect my system?
faqs.answer: 3G units have already stopped working. 2G units will stop working by 2033 at the latest. Any new unit should be 4G with voice over 4G (VoLTE) support.

faqs.question: How many people can I add?
faqs.answer: Usually hundreds and often thousands of numbers, depending on the model. Each one can be given time limits or removed individually.

faqs.question: Can I open the gate from abroad?
faqs.answer: Yes. If your phone can make a call or use the app, it can open the gate from anywhere.

keypad-entry-systems.title: Keypad Entry Systems
keypad-entry-systems.description: A keypad for your automated gate, with a separate code for each family member, cleaner or trade, and codes you can delete when access is no longer needed.
sections: Wired or wireless

A wired keypad is connected by cable to your gate’s control panel and runs off the same power supply. It’s the most reliable option and needs no batteries. If the keypad sits on a post away from the pillar, though, a cable duct has to be laid under the driveway or verge. On a new installation that’s simple to plan in. On a finished block-paved drive it means lifting and relaying a strip of paving.

A wireless keypad runs on batteries and sends a coded radio signal to a receiver in the control panel. There’s no digging, so it’s the usual choice when you’re adding a keypad to a gate that’s already installed. Expect to change the batteries roughly every one to two years. On very thick brick pillars or long driveways the signal range needs testing on site first.

There’s also the question of where the codes are stored. A standalone keypad stores them itself and is programmed at the keypad. An app-managed keypad lets you add, delete and schedule codes from your phone, which is useful if you’re often away or let the property.
Codes, users and visitors

Basic keypads hold a handful of codes. Better models hold hundreds, each one separate, so you can remove the cleaner’s access without changing the code the family uses. Some also support time windows (a code that only works on Tuesday mornings, for example), codes that expire on a set date, and a log of which code was used and when.

When we hand the system over, we suggest six-digit codes rather than four. We also suggest a separate code for each regular visitor and a lockout after several wrong entries. We change the installer’s default master code in front of you, so nobody but you can reprogramme the keypad. Codes you give to people outside the household should be changed every so often. Worn buttons on a keypad that’s been used for years can show which numbers are in the code.
Where the keypad goes

For drivers, the keypad goes on a gooseneck post on the driver’s side, at roughly car-window height (about a metre). It’s set back far enough that the car waits clear of the gate while it opens. This matters most with outward-opening swing gates, where the post has to sit beyond the arc of the gate leaves. For people on foot, a keypad on the pillar beside a pedestrian gate at about chest height works well.

Many London front gardens are shallow. If there’s no room for a car to pull off the road before the gate, a driver using a keypad ends up waiting across the pavement. In that case a remote or ANPR for residents, with the keypad kept for visitors on foot, is often a better arrangement. If you’re in a conservation area, check our borough planning guides before adding a post to the front of the property.

Keypads facing the street need backlit keys for use after dark, a rain hood, and a rating of IP65 or higher for weather sealing. Where vandalism is a concern, look for an impact rating of IK08 or above.
Adding a keypad to an existing gate

Most gate control panels from the main brands (BFT, CAME, FAAC, Nice and others) have an input that a keypad can trigger, so adding one is usually straightforward. On the survey we check that the control panel has a spare input and enough power, we plan the cable or radio route, and we test the gate’s safety devices. A keypad is another way to start the gate moving. It does nothing to stop the gate hitting a person or a car. That’s the job of the photocells and safety edges required under BS EN 12453, and we won’t connect a keypad to a gate that isn’t safe to run automatically.

If the power goes off, a keypad on mains power stops working along with the gate, unless the system has battery backup. Make sure everyone who needs to get in knows how to release the gate manually, or has a key to the pedestrian gate.
Cost of keypad entry for electric gates in London

As a rough guide, a wireless keypad added to an existing automated gate typically costs £250 to £450 fitted. A wired keypad on a gooseneck post, including ducting and making good, usually comes to £500 to £1,000, depending on distance and the surface that has to be cut. App-managed keypads with scheduling and access logs sit at the upper end or above. We give a fixed written price after the survey.
Keypad, intercom or phone entry?

A keypad suits people you trust to let themselves in. If you want to see and speak to visitors before opening the gate, look at video intercoms. If you’d rather open the gate from your mobile wherever you are, GSM phone entry does that, and many homes combine it with a keypad. For couriers specifically, see our parcel delivery access guide.

faqs.question: Can I give a delivery driver or tradesperson a temporary code?
faqs.answer: Yes, with a keypad that supports timed or expiring codes. You set the code to work for a set period and it stops working after that. Basic standalone keypads can’t do this, so tell us at survey stage if you need it.

faqs.question: How many codes can a keypad hold?
faqs.answer: It depends on the model. Entry-level keypads hold a few codes, while mid-range and app-managed units hold hundreds, each separate from the others.

faqs.question: What if someone finds out a code?
faqs.answer: Delete that code or change it. You don’t need to change anyone else’s, as long as each person has their own code. A lockout after repeated wrong entries stops anyone trying codes until one works.

faqs.question: Does the keypad work in a power cut?
faqs.answer: Only if the gate has battery backup. Otherwise use the manual release or the pedestrian gate key until power is restored.

faqs.question: Can you fit a keypad to a gate someone else installed?
faqs.answer: Usually, yes. We check the control panel, the power supply and the gate’s safety devices on the survey first.

pedestrian-side-gates.title: Pedestrian and Side Gates
pedestrian-side-gates.description: Pedestrian and side gates for London properties. Plan a usable walking route with the opening, lock, privacy and fitting details suited to your entrance.
sections: How wide should it be?

Think about everything that needs to pass through, not just people. Most front pedestrian gates are 900 mm to 1 metre wide. For wheelchair access, aim for at least 850 mm of clear opening once the gate is hung. That’s measured between the open gate and the opposite post, not the width of the gate itself, because the hinges, the stop and the thickness of the open leaf all take space. Double buggies need about the same.

Side passage gates have extra traffic. A standard wheelie bin is around 600 mm wide, but you’ll want room to wheel it without scraping your knuckles, and to get bikes, lawnmowers and building materials through. If the passage allows, 1 metre or more makes everyday life easier. Communal bins on blocks of flats are much wider and usually need a double gate.
Securing a side passage

Police crime-prevention advice on side gates is consistent. Fit the gate as close to the front of the house as possible, so there’s no hidden recess for someone to work in. Make it at least 1.8 metres tall, with no horizontal rails or cross-braces on the outside to climb. Lock it from the inside. Hinges should have pins that can’t be knocked out, or be fixed with security screws. A solid boarded timber or steel-framed gate with a top rail at the same height as the fences either side is far harder to get over than a low gate with a trellis top. Our driveway and home security guide covers the rest of the frontage.
Locks, latches and closers

For a side gate, a key-operated lock with a thumb-turn on the inside is the most practical setup. You can lock it from the garden without a key and open it from the street with one. Add heavy-duty bolts top and bottom on the inside for extra security when you’re away.

For a front pedestrian gate, a gate lock with handles on both sides lets you open it normally and lock it at night. Traditional timber gates often use a Suffolk latch or ring latch for a period look.

A hydraulic gate closer brings the gate shut automatically and stops it slamming. That’s useful if you have children or a dog, or if visitors and delivery drivers never shut gates behind them. Closers have to be matched to the gate’s weight and paired with a latch that catches reliably as the gate closes. A closer fighting a stiff latch leaves the gate open. Self-closing hinges are a simpler, cheaper option for light gates.
Electric locks and entry systems

A pedestrian gate can be fitted with an electric lock and opened by an intercom, keypad, fob reader or GSM phone entry. That’s how most homes let visitors in without walking down to the gate.

There are two main types of electric lock, and the difference matters if the power fails. A magnetic lock holds the gate shut only while it’s powered, so it releases in a power cut. That’s the safe choice on any gate that people may need to leave through in an emergency, such as the entrance to a block of flats. An electric strike or solenoid lock stays locked when the power goes, which is more secure but must always have a manual way to open it from the inside. From inside, people leave by a handle, a push-to-exit button or both. On shared entrances and escape routes, the arrangement must allow everyone out quickly in a fire, so it needs to be agreed with whoever manages the building.

Electric locks need a cable to the gate, usually in a duct under the path. Planning it at the same time as the driveway gate automation saves digging twice. See access control systems.
Separate gate or wicket door?

A separate pedestrian gate has its own opening beside the driveway gates. It’s the better option if there’s room. It gives a level walking route, works independently of the vehicle gates, and lets people walk in without stepping into the path of a moving gate.

A wicket is a small door built into one leaf of a larger gate. It’s useful where there’s no space for a separate opening, and is common on large timber gates and commercial entrances. The drawbacks are a raised threshold (often a step-over bottom rail, which is awkward for buggies and wheelchairs unless a low-threshold design is used) and a narrower opening. On a powered gate, a wicket needs a safety switch so the main gate can’t move while the wicket is open. It’s an important safeguard that cheaper installations sometimes leave out.
Materials and matching

Pedestrian gates are made in every material we use for driveway gates: timber and hardwood, steel and wrought iron style, aluminium and composite. If you’re also having driveway gates made, ordering the pedestrian gate at the same time keeps the colour, board pattern, bar spacing and finials identical. Matching an existing gate later is possible, but a perfect match is harder, especially with weathered timber or older ironwork.
Fitting

Side gates in London are often hung between a house wall and a neighbour’s fence or wall. They can be fixed with hinge plates into sound brickwork, or with a steel or timber post where the masonry won’t take the load. The gate should open inwards, away from the street. Where the ground rises behind the gate, the gate has to be set high enough to clear the slope, or hung on rising hinges. A small gap under the gate and attention to drainage stop water pooling or the bottom rail rotting.
Planning permission

Under permitted development rules, gates next to a road or footpath can usually be up to 1 metre high without planning permission. Gates elsewhere, such as a side gate set back from the pavement, can usually be up to 2 metres. Conservation areas, listed buildings and Article 4 directions (which remove some permitted development rights) can restrict this further. See our borough planning guides.
Cost of pedestrian and side gates in London

As a rough guide, a timber side gate typically costs £350 to £900 supplied and fitted. A steel or aluminium side gate is usually £600 to £1,500. A pedestrian gate made to match new driveway gates generally adds £800 to £2,000 to the project, depending on material and design. Adding an electric lock with a keypad or intercom typically costs £800 to £2,500, depending on the system and cable route. Our gate quotation checklist helps when comparing quotes for the whole entrance.

faqs.question: Can the pedestrian gate match my driveway gates?
faqs.answer: Yes. Made at the same time, it can match the material, colour, infill pattern and details exactly. Matching an older gate is usually possible too, though weathered timber and historic ironwork can take more work.

faqs.question: What width should a pedestrian gate be?
faqs.answer: Usually 900 mm to 1 metre for a front path gate, with at least 850 mm of clear opening if wheelchair users need access. Side passage gates benefit from 1 metre or more for bins and bikes.

faqs.question: Can I use an intercom or keypad with a side gate?
faqs.answer: Yes, with an electric lock. Choose a lock type that suits what should happen in a power cut, and make sure there’s always an easy way to open the gate from inside.

faqs.question: How tall should a side gate be for security?
faqs.answer: At least 1.8 metres, with no climbable rails on the outside, and fitted as close to the front of the house as possible.

faqs.question: Should I choose a separate gate or a wicket in the driveway gate?
faqs.answer: A separate gate if there’s room. It gives a level, independent walking route. A wicket is a good fallback where space is tight, but expect a threshold to step over and a narrower opening.

industrial-security-gates.title: Industrial Security Gates
industrial-security-gates.description: Industrial gates take more punishment than anything on a domestic drive. They open dozens or hundreds of times a day, they have lorries reversing near them, and they may be the only thing between your stock and a thief with an angle grinder. We design, supply and install sliding, speed and swing gates, palisade and mesh fencing, and access control for warehouses, depots, yards, builders’ merchants and industrial estates across London.
sections: Choosing the right gate type

Cantilever sliding gates are the standard choice for industrial entrances. The gate hangs from rollers on posts beside the opening instead of running on a ground track, so grit, ice, pallets and debris can’t jam it. A single leaf can span a very wide opening, comfortably wide enough for an articulated lorry. The trade-off is space. The gate needs a straight run alongside the fence, longer than the opening itself, because part of the frame acts as a counterweight. Our heavy-duty sliding gates page covers these in more detail.

Tracked sliding gates run on a rail set in the ground. They need less run-back than a cantilever gate, but the track has to be kept clear. That makes them a weaker choice for yards with loose material or heavy plant crossing the threshold.

Speed gates are bi-folding gates driven by powerful motors. They open in a few seconds rather than the 20 to 30 seconds a typical sliding gate takes. They suit busy entrances where vehicles would otherwise queue onto the road, and sites where tailgating through a slow-closing gate is a security problem. They fold back within their own posts, so they need very little side space. They cost more than a sliding gate.

Swing gates are the cheapest powered option and work where there’s room for the leaves to open fully without clashing with waiting or turning vehicles. Wide leaves with solid infill catch the wind badly, so on exposed sites they need heavier hinges and operators, or a different gate type.

Barriers control vehicles but don’t secure a perimeter. Many sites use a barrier for the busy working day and a gate to lock the site at night. See car park barriers.
Security ratings

If your insurer, landlord or tender asks for a rated gate, you’ll normally see one of two standards. LPS 1175 (from the Loss Prevention Certification Board) rates how long a gate or fence resists a deliberate forced attack, and with what tools. Lower ratings cover hand tools; higher ones cover extended attack with powered cutting equipment. Hostile vehicle mitigation ratings (PAS 68, IWA 14 and ISO 22343) are crash-tested ratings for stopping a vehicle being driven through the entrance. They’re usually only needed for critical infrastructure and high-risk sites.

A rating applies to the exact tested product, including its posts, foundations and locking. A heavy-looking palisade gate isn’t rated just because it looks strong. If you need a rating, we’ll supply the certification for the specific gate and configuration in the quote.

Most sites don’t need a formal rating. For them, the practical choices are what count: anti-climb mesh (358 mesh is the common high-security standard) or triple-pointed steel palisade, a height of 2.4 to 3 metres, no horizontal rails on the outside to climb, and shrouded hinges and locks that can’t easily be cut.
Planning for lorries and busy periods

Tell us the largest vehicle that uses the entrance and how it arrives. A 16.5-metre articulated lorry needs room to swing in. It also needs somewhere to wait while the gate opens that isn’t across the pavement or the road. On many London sites, that means setting the gate back from the boundary so the longest vehicle can stand clear of the highway.

Peak traffic matters as much as total traffic. A depot where 20 vans return at the end of a shift needs a faster gate and smarter access control than a warehouse with the same number of movements spread across the day. Motors are selected for their duty rating, meaning how many cycles an hour they can run without overheating. That’s why a domestic gate motor fails quickly on an industrial site.

Keep people on foot separate from vehicles. A pedestrian gate or turnstile beside the vehicle entrance stops staff and visiting drivers walking through the path of a moving gate.
Access control for staff, fleet and visitors

ANPR cameras open the gate automatically for registered vehicles. They’re ideal for fleet and staff parking (see ANPR systems). Staff on foot use fobs or cards, which can be cancelled individually and can log who came in and when. Visiting drivers use an intercom to reception or the gatehouse. For lorries, the intercom needs a second, higher panel at cab height, so the driver doesn’t have to climb down onto a live entrance.

On multi-tenant industrial estates, an intercom with a directory lets visitors call the right unit. Each tenant manages their own staff fobs, and the estate manager controls the gate itself.
Installation on a working site

Most industrial sites can’t simply close for a week. We phase the work so one side of the entrance stays usable, put temporary fencing in overnight where the perimeter is opened up, and schedule groundworks and gate hanging around your deliveries and shift patterns. Before work starts, we agree a method statement covering traffic management, pedestrian routes and who on your side is the point of contact. Heavier gates and fast motors may need a new three-phase or upgraded power supply. We identify that at survey so it doesn’t hold up the programme.

At handover you get operating instructions, training for the people who’ll run the entrance, safety test records and a log of who controls access permissions.
Cost of industrial security gates in London

As a rough guide, a powered cantilever sliding gate for a typical industrial entrance costs £12,000 to £30,000 installed, depending on width, height, foundations and access control. Speed gates usually cost £20,000 to £45,000. LPS 1175 rated gates cost significantly more than unrated equivalents. Every quote is itemised and fixed in writing after survey.
Servicing and breakdowns

High-use gates wear quickly and should be serviced every quarter, with safety devices and closing forces tested at each visit. Under HSE guidance on powered gates, the site operator is responsible for keeping them safe, and written service records are your evidence that you have. We offer service contracts with the visit frequency and breakdown response times set out in writing. For a gate that’s already faulty, see gate repair and servicing.

faqs.question: Can you supply a gate with an LPS 1175 rating?
faqs.answer: Yes. Tell us the rating your insurer or specification requires, and the quote will include the certification for the exact gate and configuration.

faqs.question: Is emergency call-out included?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. Breakdown response is part of a service contract, with the response times and charges set out in writing. Sites that can’t operate with the gate down usually choose a contract with a guaranteed response.

faqs.question: What should we have ready for the survey?
faqs.answer: A site plan if you have one, the largest vehicle using the entrance, your operating hours and busiest periods, and how staff, visitors and deliveries currently get in. It also helps to know who will sign off the specification and who will manage the gate afterwards.

faqs.question: Can you replace the gate but keep our existing fencing?
faqs.answer: Often, yes. We check the condition of the posts and fence at survey, because a powered industrial gate puts far more load on its supports than a manual one.
